title: The Architecture of Manifestation: The Ritam Diagram and the Three Strands
reflection: Find the three strands in one breath: the shape, the pulse and the stillness beneath them. Give it sixty seconds.

questions.q: What are the three strands found inside a single breath, according to Conversation 4.2?
o: A shape that holds, a rhythm that pulses, and a stillness that holds both together.
A beginning, a middle and an end, which follow one another in a fixed order.
The body, the mind and the spirit, which are separate and take turns to lead.
Three kinds of breath, slow, medium and fast, each suited to a different state.
questions.e: Inside one breath are the chest and its structures (shape), the in and out (rhythm) and the quiet centre, the awareness watching (stillness). These are the three threads of living structure, which the contemplative Sāṅkhya vision calls the guṇas: tamas, rajas and sattva.
questions.c: One breath holds shape, rhythm and stillness together

questions.q: On the Ritam Diagram, what does the doubling loop 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 5 stand for?
o: Darkness and dullness, which are the heavy side of the mind and its failure.
Form: the pattern of a shape that replicates and holds, as in cells and crystals.
Restlessness, which is the quick side of the mind and the one that wears it out.
Stillness, which is the quiet centre that holds all the other numbers in place.
questions.e: Form, or tamas, is the doubling loop: double 8 to get 16 and 1+6 is 7, and the digits close into six numbers forever. It is persistence and structure in cell division, branching trees, crystal and skeleton, and not darkness.
questions.c: The doubling loop is Form: persistence and structure, not darkness

questions.q: A woman wants to settle herself right now and asks why the breath is the place to start. How does Conversation 4.2 answer?
o: Rhythm is the strand within reach, and the breath is its handle.
The breath is the deepest of the strands, and nothing lies beyond it.
Only the breath has been studied by medicine, so it is the only one that counts.
The breath replaces attention and discernment, which are then not needed.
questions.e: Every such form pulses at its own natural frequency, so two can fall into step and many can lock into coherence. Of the strands, rhythm can be taken hold of immediately, and the breath opens the door. It is the entry and not the destination: lasting work is one-pointed attention and awakened discernment, developed in Module 5.
questions.c: Rhythm is the strand within reach, and the breath is its handle

questions.q: A class goes heavy and inert and will not engage. Which correction fits the three strands of Conversation 4.2?
o: Add a little movement, since the holding strand is dominating and rhythm is missing.
Add silence, since a class that is heavy needs still more stillness to set it right.
Add stricter rules, since a heavy room is always a room in which discipline has failed.
Add nothing, since a heavy class will lift of itself by the end of the lesson.
questions.e: Some days a class goes inert, the holding strand dominating. The gentlest correction is a little movement to lift it; a wild class needs a slow collective breath to settle. Diagnose the room as too heavy or too fast and then add the missing strand.
questions.c: A heavy room needs rhythm added; a wild room needs settling

questions.q: A woman looks at a person at home and asks only, “Which strand is loud today?” What is she practising, in the terms of Conversation 4.2?
o: Grading the person as good, middling or poor, so that she knows how to treat them.
Seeing which way the weave has leaned, without fixing or grading anyone.
Finding the cause of the person’s mood, so that it can be removed straight away.
Predicting what the person will do next, so that she can be ready for it.
questions.e: Sarah’s practice is to look at one person, or herself, and name which strand is loud: heavy and stuck, or wound up and scattered. It is learning to see which way the weave has leaned. It is not diagnosing, fixing or calling anyone good or bad.
questions.c: Name which strand is loud, without grading anyone

questions.q: “Tamas, rajas and sattva are three grades of mind, bad, middling and good, and the aim is to climb from the first to the last.”
questions.e: They are three strands, not three grades. All three are indispensable: without form there is no body, without rhythm no heartbeat, and stillness alone is an empty axis. Health is the weave, all three in proportion for this person, now.
questions.c: The strands are three threads of a weave, not three grades

questions.q: A man seems calm and withdrawn, and his friends call him serene. He has stopped engaging with anything. What does Conversation 4.2 suggest this may be?
o: True stillness, since a calm person who needs nothing is the aim of the practice.
Withdrawal dressed as stillness: tamasic drift in contemplative clothing.
Sattva, because the lack of restlessness shows that rajas has been overcome.
A matter of temperament, which should never be questioned by others.
questions.e: Genuine practice makes a person more available to life, not less. Withdrawal that looks sattvic can be tamasic drift in contemplative clothing. The diagnostic question is never which strand is good but which is over- or under-expressed right now.
questions.c: Withdrawal can look like stillness; real practice makes you more available

questions.q: “The torus, a doughnut shape with a still axis through its centre, is the one shape of all natural forms.”
questions.e: Swamiji presents the torus as one deep recurring form of life, seen in the heart’s blood vortex, a smoke ring and a hurricane’s eye, because it is a self-feeding shape. It is explicitly not the only shape in nature.
questions.c: The torus is one recurring form of life, not the only shape

questions.q: A scientist wants to check the diagram for herself instead of taking it on trust. What does Conversation 4.2 suggest?
o: Take the doubling and digit-adding further, and confirm the loop closes on six numbers.
Ask a teacher to confirm that the diagram is correct, and then accept it as it stands.
Look for the diagram in other books, and accept it if a few of them agree with it.
Leave the diagram alone, since a diagram of this kind cannot be checked by anyone.
questions.e: Kai’s exercise is to take the doubling-and-add-the-digits trick past where the lesson stopped, and confirm that the form loop is just those six numbers and that three only ever bounces to six. It is meant to be verified, not taken on trust.
questions.c: Verify the maths yourself: the loop closes on six numbers

questions.q: “Health is the three strands in proportion for this person now, while illness is the weave pulled out of proportion: too much holding, or movement outrunning structure.”
questions.e: Tamasic drift is too much holding and too little movement, as in depression; rajasic drift is movement outrunning structure, as in anxiety, panic and burnout. The reading is structural and not a verdict on the person.
questions.c: Illness is the weave pulled out of proportion
